name: Jade Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a cardboard box plant on the edge of town, running a rotary die-cutter. That's the machine that cuts and creases the flat cardboard so it folds into a box. I set the feed, watch for jams and crushed edges, and pull samples to check the fold lines. I've been there about a year and I'm still learning how to tweak it when the board is damp.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The people are good, and the pay is better than most box plants because we do a lot of overtime for the online shops. What wears me down is the dust, and the way a whole order can go wrong if I set the board wrong at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get oversold. I'd probably joke about it in the group chat with my sister. I use a chatbot sometimes for recipes, so I wouldn't say it was useless either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means we stay on track. My partner Sam is an electrician, and we've got about eight months of pay saved, plus a separate house deposit fund. If nothing changes, we buy a small house in about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the overtime, because that's what's building the deposit. Ask the shift lead to teach me how to deal with damp board, because that's where I lose time. Keep the savings steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring one, and boring is fine when you're saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The overtime depends on the online shops. If people buy less online, the extra shifts go first, and that's a big part of our deposit money. It happened for a few months last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the overtime dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd push the house back six months, that's all. It's annoying, not scary. Sam's work is steady, and I could pick up shifts at the other box plant if I had to.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, as these things usually are.
I'd admit I use a chatbot for **recipes**, so it isn't useless either.
think: Privately, we stay on track to buy a **small house** in about two years.
My partner's electrician work plus **eight months** saved keeps us steady.
do: Keep working **overtime** to build the house deposit.
Ask the shift lead to teach her how to handle **damp board**.
feel: She feels **calm**, because boring is fine while saving for a **house**.
S0.quote: Boring is fine when you're saving for a house.
fieldNote: Her plans revolve around a **house deposit**, built partly on overtime.
The real risk she names is **online shopping** slowing, not AI.
Losing overtime would be **annoying**, not scary, given her partner's steady work.

steps.text: Keep taking the online-order overtime shifts
Keep adding to the house deposit fund every month
Learn from the shift lead how to cut damp board

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to keep an eye on it but not to panic. At work I'd say the office will feel it first. I'd share the odd article in the group chat, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd watch the planners. Our orders and machine schedules are already on a computer, and AI could plan them faster. On the floor, I'd expect a robot that stacks the bundles onto pallets within a few years, and that's a person off each shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to cross-train on the bigger die-cutter, so I'm not just one machine. Once a couple of people at work found an AI tool useful for checking fold specs, I'd try it too. We'd keep buying the house, maybe just a slightly cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks okay, but you'd feel the ground moving a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a cheaper house. Why not wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rents keep going up, and waiting costs money too. We'd want a mortgage my partner could pay on his wage alone. That's our rule anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your shift would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who does the palletising by hand. He's fast and he's proud of it. A stacking robot is aimed right at his job.

say: I'd say keep an **eye on it** but don't panic.
At work I'd point out the **office** will feel it first.
think: AI could plan our **orders and schedules** faster than the planners do.
A **stacking robot** would take one person off each shift within a few years.
do: Ask to **cross-train** on the bigger die-cutter.
Try an **AI tool** for fold specs once colleagues find it useful.
Buy a slightly **cheaper house** with a mortgage her partner's wage alone could cover.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, sensing the **ground moving** a little.
S1.quote: We'd want a mortgage my partner could pay on his wage alone.
fieldNote: She sees the **planners** as exposed first, and palletising next.
Her **mortgage rule** is a quiet hedge against her own job.
She'd adopt AI only after **colleagues** prove it useful.

steps.text: Cross-train on the bigger die-cutter this year
Try an AI tool for fold specs after colleagues use it
Buy a cheaper house that Sam's wage alone could cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and the government needs to step up with something real. I wouldn't go to protests, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan. At work I'd be telling people to sort their money out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone by 2031. A robot that feeds board and checks for crushed edges is not hard, and box plants run on thin margins, so they'd buy it the minute it's cheap. The AI in 2028 would take the planners first, and then our side follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pause the house for a year until we see how fast things move. Ask Sam whether I could train as an electrician's mate with him, because wiring a house is harder for a robot. Keep the savings untouched and stop the overtime spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because Sam's work is hands-on and we've got savings, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't protest. What would push you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they took the money people paid in and gave nothing back. Like cutting retraining help to pay for tax breaks for robot buyers. That would get me out on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to get out of her call centre job now, before 2028. Answering phones is the first thing to go in this one.

say: I'd say the government needs to step up with something **real**.
I'd skip protests but **vote** for whoever had an actual plan.
think: My die-cutting job is probably **gone by 2031**; box plants run on thin margins.
The **2028 AI** takes the planners first, then robots reach our side.

Ask her partner about training as an **electrician's mate**.
Keep **savings** untouched and stop spending the overtime money.
feel: She feels **anxious** but not panicking, because her partner's work is hands-on.

fieldNote: She reasons from **thin margins** to fast robot buying, a sharp read.

Her worry spreads to her sister's **call centre** job.

steps.text: Pause the house purchase for at least a year
Train as an electrician's mate with Sam before 2031
Stop spending overtime pay and keep savings untouched
Vote for the party with a clear retraining plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people stop arguing and start planning. I'd tell friends to look at hands-on trades. I'd still keep it calm, no doom posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years suits me. The AI in 2031 hits the office, the robots in 2034 hit us, and by then I could be qualified as an electrician. Sam would help, and we'd have done it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the house as planned, with the Sam's-wage-alone rule. Start an electrical apprenticeship around 2028, once I've seen how the robot rollout is going at other plants. Use the AI tools for studying, once they're proven for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a route through, and that helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the box plant early, before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around 2029, yes, because the apprenticeship pay is low and I'd want to do it while we still have the overtime money saved. Leaving early beats being pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins who are about to leave school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots will be slow at awkward places, so learn something where you have to crawl into a loft or under a floor. That's what I'd tell my cousins.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if people stop arguing and start planning.
I'd tell friends to look at **hands-on trades**, without posting doom.
think: The **2034 robots** hit us, but I could be a qualified electrician by then.
With my partner helping, we'd have done it **properly**.
do: Buy the **house** as planned with the one-wage mortgage rule.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** around 2028 after watching other plants.
Leave the box plant around **2029**, before being pushed out.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but steadied by seeing a **route** through.
S3.quote: Robots will be slow at awkward places, so learn something where you have to crawl into a loft or under a floor.
fieldNote: With five years she has a **concrete route**, so her mood drops to uneasy.
She'd leave **voluntarily** before robots arrive, on her own terms.
Her advice for the young is **awkward physical** work.

steps.text: Buy the house with a mortgage Sam's wage could cover
Leave the box plant around 2029 for electrical work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's use it well. At work I'd say there's no need to panic but no excuse not to plan. I'd probably talk about it more than post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels comfortable. I could stay at the box plant until the mid-2030s, buy the house, maybe have a baby, and then switch. The robots arrive in 2039 and I'd be 40, which is fine for a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the house next year. Keep doing the overtime. Start part-time electrical training around 2031, and use AI tools for studying once they're normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, in the background. It wouldn't stop me planning a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw a stacking robot go in at our plant early. That would tell me the robots were coming sooner than the card says. Then I'd start training straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone who would struggle more than you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads who've done die-cutting for twenty years. Ten years is long for me, but for the older die-cutters it lands right before retirement, which is the worst time.

At work I'd say there's **no excuse** not to plan, but no need to panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Box plants would buy the robots fast, and I'd be retraining at the same time as everyone. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage, so people like me don't have to burn through savings to switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the house matters. Every picture you read out, my first thought was whether we could still buy a house.

headlineQuote: Every picture you read out, my first thought was whether we could still buy a house.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** die-cutter operator at a cardboard box plant, a year in.
She and her electrician partner have **eight months** saved plus a house deposit fund.
She tries new tools once **others prove** them, and plans around a one-wage mortgage.
She moves from calm to **anxious** at AGI by 2028, with **electrical work** as her route.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because box plants would buy **robots fast** and everyone would retrain at once.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships that pay a **proper wage**, so switching doesn't burn through savings.
